assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are the workhorse of modern monetary policy analysis. Staggered pricing and contracts, policy rules and the microfounded synthesis shape central-bank practice and research worldwide. Few macro contributions have had comparable breadth of influence.
assessment.attribution: Calvo (time-dependent pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule) and Woodford (the integrated microfounded framework and its normative analysis) are the most defensible three. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets are major contributors, particularly on estimation and DSGE quantification, but a three-person cap forces hard choices. Attribution is crowded and some credit is inevitably left out.
assessment.maturity: The core contributions date from the 1980s to the early 2000s and have decades of validation in theory and practice. The post-2021 inflation episode tested the framework and left it standing, though not unscathed.
uncertainties: Crowded credit; Gali, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum have strong claims too.
Some of the framework's empirical weaknesses (the Phillips curve, the role of heterogeneity) are still debated.
The macroeconomics field may be seen as recently rewarded, though not for this topic.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political economics built a systematic, empirically testable theory of how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and development. It turned a loose field into a core part of mainstream economics and has been widely applied.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central pair, with the books and papers on electoral rules and constitutions. Besley's work on state capacity and accountability is a large complementary contribution. The three-person set is natural and coherent.
assessment.maturity: The contributions span three decades and have been confirmed in many empirical settings. The literature has been recognised repeatedly in the discipline. The case is mature, and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Persson is an IIES colleague of the assessing member. This is a disclosed institutional proximity, not adjudicated here.
Some causal claims on constitutions rest on contested identification.
Competing claims from other political-economy theorists could split support.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm trade framework reoriented the field around firm-level selection and productivity. It changed how gains from trade are measured and how trade policy is understood. It is a clear conceptual advance with empirical grounding.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the pivotal model. Helpman's earlier work on increasing returns and monopolistic competition, and his later firm-heterogeneity work, make him a natural co-recipient. Redding has important contributions, but the core credit is concentrated in two names. Bernard, Eaton and Kortum, among others, are close precursors outside this ballot entry.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation across many datasets and countries. The framework is a textbook staple.
uncertainties: Helpman also appears in another ballot entry, so this candidacy overlaps with it.
Melitz's contribution is largely a single seminal paper, with credit shared with the broader firm-heterogeneity literature.
Quantitative trade models may be judged to have superseded some of the framework.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Using population-scale administrative data, this work established new facts about intergenerational mobility and its geographic variation. It also developed causal designs for neighbourhood effects, and it has strongly influenced policy debate and empirical practice.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the leading figure and Hendren is the key co-author on the causal neighbourhood-effects work. Friedman and Katz contribute significantly, but credit concentrates in the first two. Chetty also appears on other ballot entries, so the overall body of work extends beyond this entry.
assessment.maturity: The core results date from about 2014 onward. Replication and follow-up are substantial, but long-term validation is still under way, so the case is less mature than the older candidates.
uncertainties: The work is recent, and the interpretation of place effects is still being tested.
Credit could instead be framed around Chetty's broader portfolio.
Data-access and team-based credit questions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Kiyotaki–Moore model of collateral constraints, credit cycles and amplification became the template for macro-financial propagation. It is central to post-2008 analysis of financial frictions and a foundation of modern financial-macro modelling.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the joint authors of the 1997 credit-cycles paper, which makes the pairing clean. The financial-accelerator tradition (Bernanke, Gertler, Gilchrist) is related but distinct. Bernanke has already been recognised, and the ballot's Gertler and Gilchrist claims sit with that parallel line.
assessment.maturity: The 1997 paper has nearly three decades of influence, and the 2008 crisis strongly reinforced its relevance.
uncertainties: Overlap with the financial-accelerator tradition could split credit.
The paper is highly stylised, and its empirical quantification is mixed.
A macro-finance award might be judged against other candidates in the same area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law and finance made legal institutions and investor protection a central explanation of financial development and corporate governance. It created a very large cross-country empirical research programme.
assessment.attribution: The LLSV collaboration is a tight, well-defined group. Vishny's role is also significant but belongs more to the earlier corporate-finance work, so I credit the three most associated with the legal-origins agenda.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the late 1990s and has had long influence, but its core claims have also been challenged.
uncertainties: Legal-origins identification and measurement have been seriously questioned.
Data and replication critiques of the anti-director-rights indices.
Shleifer's broader body of work might suggest different grouping.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model gave a strategic foundation for bargaining and bargaining in markets, and it is widely used in applied theory across labour, trade, industrial organisation and macroeconomics. It is a fundamental theoretical building block.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the central contribution. Wolinsky (with Rubinstein) extended it to markets with search and decentralised trade. Binmore's contribution is real, but it is more of a parallel and later development.
assessment.maturity: More than four decades of use. The theory is well settled and the case is mature.
uncertainties: Game-theory recognition has been frequent, which might lower priority.
Contributions to decision theory and other areas by Rubinstein are not weighed here.
Binmore's claim could complicate the choice of laureates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based framework and the China-shock evidence changed understanding of how technology and trade reshape labour demand, local labour markets and inequality. It has had a large effect on research and policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the central figure across both the task framework and the trade-shock evidence. Dorn and Hanson are essential co-authors of the China-shock work. Katz's earlier skill-biased technological change work is foundational but is partly attributed on other entries. Acemoglu and Restrepo, who developed the formal task-based theory, are not on this ballot entry, which complicates the attribution.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 2000s and 2010s. Its empirical conclusions continue to be debated, but it is well replicated.
uncertainties: Task-model theory credit sits partly outside the listed names.
Results on local-market adjustment are sensitive to specification and time period.
The case is less mature than older candidates.
